summary: The deletion itself is right and I verified the hard part independently: `aBATCHEDDeltaDeliversEverySegmentFromWhereItsBytesARE` really does carry ADR-0032's property for the half that matters -- deliver pod B's run under the first segment in the batch and `fromTheirs` receives `mine`'s 4,096 bytes instead of `theirs`'s 8,192 and the test reds -- and the held-key-versus-first-index confusion is separately killed by AssembledServingPathFailureTest, which puts the held segment SECOND on purpose. The seven rewritten routing cases still constrain what they constrained, the three call sites outside `ingest` compile (I built :plugin:compileClusterTestJava) and behave identically, and the store is read zero times before and after, so the request rate is untouched. What the change does NOT do is finish the removal it names. `publishRun` -- the private method the two deleted overloads were the only callers of -- is left behind with zero callers in the tree, in a file whose own javadoc says in this same commit that M5.47 removes it; and the surviving four-argument `publish` still carries a paragraph describing the two overloads as present, including a `{@link}` to one of the methods this diff deletes. Both are inside the fifty-five lines the diff is editing, and both are false the moment it lands.

findings.title: `publishRun` is left behind with no caller anywhere, and the file's own javadoc says this commit removes it
findings.failure_scenario: `private void publishRun(String, RunCommit, byte[])` at :478 was called from exactly two places -- the two overloads this diff deletes. I grepped the whole tree after the deletion: the only remaining occurrences of the name are javadoc (:68, SegmentProxy.java:102, SegmentProxyFailureTest.java:41, AssembledServingPathFailureTest.java:267) and the declaration itself. javac does not error on an unused private method and no gate in the passed list looks for one, so nothing catches it. Two concrete consequences. (a) The Push javadoc at :68 reads `⚠️ {@link #publishRun} -- the pre-M5.45a path M5.47 removes -- is the one place that still carries the array in this record.` This IS M5.47, and it does not remove it; a reader of the record's contract at :46 (`segment() IS EMPTY IN EVERY PUSH THE SERVING PATH BUILDS`) is pointed at a method that is still there and still builds a Push carrying the whole array with `FetchMode.INLINE` hard-coded. (b) M5.15b and M5.15d are both queued to reshape Push/Delivery in this same file. A live-looking private method that takes `(segmentKey, run, segment)` is exactly what gets re-wired as `the simple path` by whoever lands next, and it reintroduces the mis-pairing the deleted `publish(CommitDelta, byte[])` javadoc spent a paragraph refusing: one array delivered under each run's own key, decoded by a subscriber whose stream is in another pod's segment, thrown inside the sink and swallowed by `deliver`/`pushLoop` as a slow subscriber. Silent record loss, no request, no log. Removing it is not scope widening: it is unreachable only because of this diff, the task's own argument (`each is the other's excuse for staying`) applies to it, and the file already promises its removal here.
findings.remedy: Delete `publishRun` and `EMPTY`'s remaining sole use if it becomes unused, and rewrite :68 to say the serving path is now the only builder of a Push -- or, if it is genuinely wanted for a later row, keep it and correct :68, which is the one thing that must not stay as written.

findings.title: the surviving `publish`'s javadoc still describes the two deleted overloads, with a `{@link}` to one of them
findings.failure_scenario: Two false sites in the paragraph the diff leaves untouched directly under the code it deletes. :222 reads `{@link #publish(CommitDelta, byte[])} above takes a bare {@code byte[]} and REFUSES any delta naming more than one segment` -- there is no such method after this commit, so the reference resolves to nothing. No `javadoc` task is configured in `buildSrc/src/main/kotlin/binjava.java-conventions.gradle.kts`, so nothing fails today; the standard doclint errors `reference not found` on an unresolvable `@link`, so this becomes a build failure the day a javadoc or publish task is added, and until then it sends a reader to a method that is not in the file. :231-233 is worse because it is a statement about the file's present state: `⚠️ THE TWO OVERLOADS ABOVE NOW HAVE NO PRODUCTION CALLER and M5.47 removes them; they are still reachable from {@code ingest}'s tests, so this is a live method next to two dead ones rather than a choice.` After this commit there are no overloads above, nothing is reachable from `ingest`'s tests, and the method is not `next to two dead ones`. A reader of `SubscriptionHub` at HEAD is told the class has three publish methods when it has one, and goes looking for the refusal path when debugging a batched delta. The substance of the paragraph -- why the held key travels with the held bytes, and why letting the refusal reach `pushLoop` drops the window -- is worth keeping; only the tense and the `@link` are wrong.
findings.remedy: Rewrite :220-233 in the past tense with no `@link`: the predecessor took a bare `byte[]` and refused a multi-segment delta, that refusal reached `pushLoop` as a slow subscriber, matching by key is the answer -- and drop the `two dead ones` sentence, which existed only to explain why they had not been deleted yet.

findings.title: `publishHeld` builds a CountingBinStore whose counters are never read, so the `zero store reads` its own javadoc claims is unasserted here
findings.failure_scenario: The helper's javadoc at :29-46 and the M5.47 State cell both make the cost claim -- `the store is read ZERO times either way`. I confirmed the claim is true (cap `Long.MAX_VALUE` and `bytesInServingAz == true` give INLINE for any size, and the INLINE arm calls `writeHeldBytes`, never `serving.proxy()`), but nothing in this file would notice if it stopped being true: mutate `case INLINE ->` to route through `streamFromStore` and all seven routing cases still pass, because `store.counts()` is never read. The property is held elsewhere -- AssembledServingPathTest.aSegmentUNDERTheInlineCapIsServedINLINEAndReadZEROTimes and proxyForBytesTheNodeHOLDSCostsZEROReads both assert the zero -- which is why this is minor rather than major, but the store object is constructed 1,600 times inside `manyIdleSubscribersIssueNoStoreRequestsAtAll`'s control loop for no observable purpose.
findings.remedy: One line at the end of `publishHeld`: `assertThat(store.counts().total()).isZero();` -- it pins the claim the helper's own javadoc makes and costs nothing.

findings.title: `small enough that FetchPolicy answers INLINE` is not why these publishes inline
findings.failure_scenario: The HELD javadoc says the three bytes are `small enough that {@link FetchPolicy} answers {@code INLINE}`. The policy built two lines below is `new FetchPolicyConfig(Long.MAX_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE, 1)`, and `FetchPolicy.modeFor` returns INLINE for `batchBytes <= inlineBound` -- with the bound at `Long.MAX_VALUE` every segment inlines, so the size of HELD decides nothing. The State cell repeats it as `three held bytes and an inline-forever policy`, which is the accurate form. Concrete failure: someone enlarging HELD to exercise a large-segment routing case reads this sentence, expects the 256 KiB default cap to flip the mode to PROXY, and gets INLINE anyway -- then debugs FetchPolicy rather than the config the helper hard-codes.
findings.remedy: Say what is true: the policy is inline-forever, so the mode is fixed regardless of size and the three bytes are merely a payload the sink can compare.

findings.title: the replacement carries ADR-0032 for the BYTES, not for the push's segmentKey label -- the claim `asserts the same ADR-0032 property` is slightly wider than the test
findings.failure_scenario: I verified the claim as asked and it holds where it counts: `aBATCHEDDeltaDeliversEverySegmentFromWhereItsBytesARE` uses two differently sized, differently valued segments and asserts `fromTheirs.bytes()).isEqualTo(theirs)`, so a run delivered under the first segment in the batch reds the test; and the adjacent `AssembledServingPathFailureTest.aSTOREFailureOnOneSegmentDoesNotDenyTheSegmentThisPodHOLDS` orders the held segment SECOND, which kills the `held bytes go to segments().get(0)` mutation the new test alone would survive. The gap: the deleted test also asserted `p.segmentKey()` and `p.firstOffset()` on the Push of each run of a MULTI-segment delta; the replacement never captures a Push, only `push.via()`. Those per-run fields are pinned for a SINGLE-segment delta by `aSegmentOfMANYRunsIsReadONCENotOncePerRun`, and under the current shape the label and the bytes both come from the same `SegmentCommit`, so I could not construct a natural mutation that mislabels one without misrouting the other -- which is why this is minor and not a lost property. It is recorded so the State cell's sentence is read as byte-level rather than label-level, since `segmentKey` is what a consumer would resolve on a restart.
findings.remedy: Either narrow the State cell to `asserts it of the BYTES each subscriber receives, which is the consequential half`, or add `assertThat(push.segmentKey())` to the two lambdas the batched test already has.

verified: The refusal deletion is justified: the four-argument `publish` has no `IllegalStateException` for a multi-segment delta -- it loops `delta.segments()` and matches `heldSegmentKey` per segment -- so `publishingABatchedDeltaWithONESharedPayloadIsRefused` asserted a throw that cannot occur. Nothing replaces it and nothing should.

The seven rewritten routing cases still constrain what they did. `aSubscriberIsNotWokenByOtherStreams` still depends on the per-RunKey map (a delta naming only B's run leaves `targets` empty and returns before any sink is opened); `aThrowingSubscriberDoesNotStopTheOthersOrTheCommit` still exercises isolation, now at `deliver`'s open loop rather than at `publishRun`'s; `aSubscriberIsPushedItsOwnStreamsCommits` reads segmentKey/firstOffset/recordCount/lastOffset off the Push that `assembling.complete` copies from the open Push, so the fields are still the ones the hub built. None of them is satisfied by the serving path instead of by routing: no assertion in the file reads `push.segment()` or any store counter.

The three call sites outside the unit tests are fine. I applied the staged diff to a throwaway worktree and ran `:plugin:compileClusterTestJava :ingest:test :plugin:test` -- BUILD SUCCESSFUL, so ShardFanOutIT and SearchableIT compile even though `./gradlew test` never touches them. Their subject is unchanged: each bridge is `SubscriptionHub.assembling(...)`, which builds a second Push carrying the assembled array, so `push.segment()` at ShardFanOutIT:74, SearchableIT:79 and EndToEndTest:72 still receives the whole segment rather than the EMPTY array the serving path opens with; and `push.via()` is INLINE both before (publishRun hard-coded `FetchMode.INLINE`) and after (inline-forever config), so SearchableIT's Delivery carries the same mode it did.

Cost lens: the request rate is unchanged and remains segment-scaled. The held key equals the delta's only segment key at all three moved call sites and in `publishHeld`, so `publishSegment` takes the INLINE arm into `writeHeldBytes` and `serving.proxy()` is never touched -- zero GETs before (publishRun issued none either) and zero after. The `new SegmentProxy(store)` built at each call site is a constructor, not a request. Nothing here adds a request that scales with records, shards, partitions or indices, and no LIST is introduced.

Scope: the diff touches only the two overloads, their callers, and the backlog row. It does not widen into M5.45b (`direct`), M5.48 (`pushLoop`'s silent drop) or M5.16, all of which the surviving javadoc still defers correctly.

Process: I read the packet and the tree only. I did not read the author's plan or transcript, I asked for no rationale, and I made no change to the working tree -- the worktree I built was a detached `git worktree` under the session scratchpad with the staged patch applied, and the staged hash is 4ce8f7294fbd both before and after my run.
